screeningScope: Full-text source, eligibility, taxonomy, and synthesis-readiness review of Training & Performance queue positions 1-95. Drafted by Claude Haiku 5.5 and claim-audited against source text by Claude Opus 5.5 (docs/haiku-calibration/).

decisionDefinitions.INCLUDE: Eligible for evidence extraction and synthesis after full-text review.
decisionDefinitions.DEGRADED: A required source or verification element was unavailable.

records.sourceFile: Personalized resistance training mitigates neuromuscular and perceived fatigue - The autoregulation cluster training method.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Randomized crossover study of 26 resistance-trained men who completed three sessions of bench press and back squat at 75% 1RM, matched for load, volume (24 repetitions) and total rest (240 s): traditional sets (TRA), interset rest redistribution (IRR) and an autoregulated cluster method (ACT) that adjusted the cluster structure to a 20% velocity loss target. IRR and ACT produced less velocity loss than TRA (b = -2.09, P < .001), ACT produced less than IRR (b = -2.31, P < .001), and rate of fatigue followed the same pattern.
records.limitations: Single-session, acute outcomes in 26 men at one load (75% 1RM), with one comparator cluster structure. No strength, hypertrophy or long-term adaptation outcomes were measured.
records.synthesisCaution: Reading lower within-session velocity loss as evidence that ACT builds more strength or muscle than traditional sets, when the study measured only acute responses.

changes: limitations: framed the -2.09 vs +2.09 sign as unresolved and called the ROF interaction paragraph garbled -> sign resolved as a text typo (abstract, Table 3 and CI '-2.46 to -1.72' all negative); the mislabelled paragraph identified as the velocity loss interaction ('P = .136; b = -0.81 ... percent loss')
limitations: 'Two authors' -> named Dello Iacono and Watson ('Dello Iacono and Watson declare conflict of interest')
findings: added that structure by exercise interactions were not significant (Table 3: -0.81, 0.34, no asterisk)

records.sourceFile: Pharmacological and physiological effects of cannabidiol - A dose escalation, placebo washout study protocol.pdf
records.exclusionReason: Not an eligible evidence type: this is a published study protocol (Neary et al., BMC Neurology 2024;24:340) for an open-label, placebo-washout, dose-escalation phase 1 CBD trial in 40 healthy male contact-sport athletes. It reports no participant data or results ('No datasets were generated or analysed during the current study'). It fails the INCLUDE test because it is not original research evidence, a review or a consensus statement. Code (b) is the closest listed reason, but (b) as worded covers pieces 'without original methods', and this protocol does describe original methods, so no listed reason fits exactly.

changes: exclusionReason: rewritten to rest on the INSTRUCTIONS eligibility rules alone, with the (b) wording mismatch made explicit; decision EXCLUDE unchanged ('No datasets were generated or analysed during the current study')
verification.residualConcerns: Operator call needed. Judged on the INSTRUCTIONS rules alone, with no library precedent assumed: a protocol with no results is not one of the four INCLUDE evidence types, so it cannot be INCLUDE, and it is not unreadable or truncated, so DEGRADED does not fit. EXCLUDE is the only available outcome, but none of reasons (a) to (c) fits cleanly: (b) excludes items without original methods, and this protocol has detailed methods. If Eric wants protocols in the library (for example to flag upcoming concussion-relevant CBD evidence in football players, NCT06204003, NFL/NFLPA-funded), it would need a new category or an 'Other' study design. The topic is clinically sensitive (cannabinoid dosing, concussion). Identity and DOI (10.1186/s12883-024-03847-1, printed on page 1) are confirmed.

records.sourceFile: Physiological Resilience - What Is It and How Might It Be Trained.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Narrative review of physiological resilience, the decline of VO2max, economy and metabolic thresholds during prolonged exercise, proposed as a fourth determinant of endurance performance. It summarises interindividual variation in critical power after 2 hours of heavy cycling (about 10% at group mean, 1% to 33% range, in non-elite participants) and reviews observational and small training studies. It suggests that consistent long-term volume, prolonged sessions with race-pace or progressive efforts, and heavy strength and plyometric training may build resilience, but no training study has tested resilience directly.
records.limitations: No literature search or appraisal method is described, and the training suggestions rest on observational data, small studies and an unpublished doctoral thesis. No longitudinal study has tested training for resilience.
records.synthesisCaution: Treating the suggested training components (long-term volume, race-pace sessions, heavy strength work) as proven ways to build resilience, when the authors say data are scant and inferences rely partly on anecdote and conjecture.

changes: synthesisCaution: 'the evidence is scant and largely anecdotal' -> scant and partly reliant on anecdote ('rely to some extent on anecdote and conjecture')

records.sourceFile: Physiological adaptations and practical efficacy of different blood flow restriction resistance training modes in athletic populations.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Review that describes a database search (CNKI, PubMed, Web of Science) of 412 articles, from which 14 studies of athletes with structured blood flow restriction (BFR) training and control groups were included. The included studies (Table 1, sample sizes 6 to 32) are summarized by three BFR modalities, and no pooled analysis is reported apart from a cited meta-analysis (Su et al. 2025).
records.limitations: The authors call this a narrative review, describe Table 1 as a representative overview rather than an exhaustive systematic inventory, and do not appraise study quality; most mechanistic statements are hypotheses drawn from the wider literature rather than from the 14 studies. Several in-text citations do not match the reference titles (for example Su et al. 2025, Wang et al. 2023, Wang et al. 2022, Lubowitz et al. 2022, Mitchell et al. 2019 and Laurentino et al. 2012), so those specific claims could not be traced to the cited studies.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff may read the mechanistic framework (fiber-type specialization by modality and a periodized phase plan) as established evidence, when the authors describe it as a preliminary framework built on small, heterogeneous studies.

changes: paper.findings: Korkmaz strength gains reported as exceeding HLRT -> noted that Table 1 marks strength as within-group only ('Knee joint MVC*' with '*Significant within-group changes but no between-group differences')
paper.findings: ES 0.65 meta-analysis labelled as BFR-LIRT evidence -> flagged that the Su et al. 2025 reference title is 'blood flow restriction combined with high-load training'
paper.findings: Che, Sarfabadi and Zhu grouped as 'S-BFRRT and C-BFRRT' -> attributed to C-BFRRT (Table 1 modality column)
paper.limitations: added Korkmaz table/text conflict and Scott 5 vs 6 week discrepancy ('no additional benefits from 5-week S-BFRRT'; table '2x/wk. For 6 wk')
screeningLimitations/methods: added authors' statement that Table 1 is 'a representative overview ... rather than ... an exhaustive systematic inventory' and Su 2025 to citation mismatches
evidenceSummary: 'cited meta-analysis of BFR-LIRT' -> 'cited meta-analysis (Su et al. 2025)'
verification.residualConcerns: studyDesign kept as Systematic Review / Meta-analysis per library precedent because a database search (412 -> 14) is described, but the authors label it a narrative review and say Table 1 is not an exhaustive inventory; a reviewer may prefer Narrative Review. Multiple in-text citations do not match the reference list.

records.sourceFile: Planned Load Reduction Versus Fixed Load- A Strategy to Reduce the Perception of Effort With Similar Improvements in Hypertrophy and Strength.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Randomized 16-week trial in 21 recreationally resistance-trained men (age 23.2 [4.2] y), assigned to constant load (CON), 5% load reduction (RED 5) or 10% load reduction (RED 10), 7 per group, training biceps curls and Scott curls to volitional fatigue 3 days per week. The authors report no between-group differences in muscle thickness, 10RM strength or volume load, and a lower average daily RPE for RED 10 than CON for the biceps curl and than CON and RED 5 for the Scott curl.
records.limitations: Groups of 7 give limited precision for the no-difference findings, and the protocol used two single-joint elbow flexor exercises with 3 sets each. The results therefore do not show how load reduction behaves in multijoint lifts or in athletes.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read the lower RPE as a sign that load reduction builds more muscle or strength, but the study found no difference in hypertrophy, strength or volume load between groups.

changes: paper.limitations: added abstract vs results conflict (abstract 'Volume load lifted ... CON, 38,495 ... P = .094' are Scott-curl values per results; abstract biceps RPE 'P = .001' vs results 'P = .002')
identityCheck: recorded that Q12 (accepted manuscript) is excluded as a duplicate and this published version is kept

records.sourceFile: Player-Level Tackle Training Interventions in Tackle-Collision Sports - A Systematic Scoping Review.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Systematic scoping review (PRISMA-ScR; four databases searched January 2000 to 30 May 2024) of player-level tackle training interventions. Thirteen studies with 503 athletes (360 in American football, 143 in rugby) were included, 11 quasi-experimental and two randomised controlled trials, and the authors report that every study showed a favorable change in its outcome measure.
records.limitations: The evidence is small and mostly short-term, with samples ranging from one case-study player to 180 participants, mostly in youth or amateur players, and many outcomes are tackle technique or head acceleration measured in laboratories rather than injury. The review did not pool effects, so the uniform 'all studies improved' conclusion is descriptive and cannot establish effect size or injury benefit.
records.synthesisCaution: Reading the finding that every intervention improved its outcome as evidence that tackle training reduces concussion or match injury would overstate it, because most studies measured technique or head impacts in controlled or training settings.

changes: paper.limitations: quality wording made precise; abstract says 'The quality of studies were rated as good' while results give only JBI scores ('average criteria score was 7 out of 9 (mode = 7, range 4-9)'; RCTs '10 out of 13' and '11'), with no threshold defining 'good'

records.sourceFile: Positional differences in muscle to bone ratio in National Football League players.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Retrospective DXA analysis of 346 NFL players scanned before drafts or training camp between 2006 and 2011, compared with 228 age-matched healthy male controls from population-based studies. NFL players had higher lean mass and bone mineral content and a lower total muscle-to-bone ratio (18.50 vs 19.12, P < .001) and trunk ratio, with no difference in leg ratio (16.72 vs 16.85); the total ratio did not differ by position, although the leg ratio did.
records.limitations: Cross-sectional, retrospective DXA data from one time point, with controls drawn from population studies rather than athletes. Only 346 of 411 measured players fit the scanner field, which may narrow the body-size range (Inference), and the abstract calls a body-fat percentage difference 'significantly lower' at P = .053, which does not meet the usual .05 threshold.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read a lower total muscle-to-bone ratio as evidence of better bone-to-muscle balance or lower bone strength in NFL players, when the paper only compares groups at one time point and reports no link to performance or injury.

changes: paper.limitations: added the abstract's 'significantly lower percent total body fat (17.90 vs 22.93%, p=0.053)' as a misstatement of significance (previously only in screeningLimitations); Results text says only 'lower %BF'. Replaced 'wet versus dry bone mass' (which the authors use to explain differences from other studies' MBR values, not the NFL vs control difference) with the height and skeleton-size explanation they actually give
populations: added Male Athletes (players 'were matched to a population of healthy males'; controls 'age-matched healthy, male')
screeningLimitations: labelled the scanner-field inference with the house 'Inference' label and clarified the P = .053 issue

records.sourceFile: Positional movement demands during NFL football games - A 3-year review.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Retrospective analysis of NFL Next Gen Stats tracking data from 768 regular-season games (2018-2020), summarized per player per game for distance, maximum velocity, high-velocity efforts and distance, and acceleration and deceleration efforts and distance. High-velocity thresholds were set at 85% of each position's 75th-percentile maximum velocity; safeties, cornerbacks and wide receivers covered the most distance and reached the highest speeds, wide receivers made the most acceleration efforts (tight ends second), linebackers the most high-velocity efforts, and linemen the lowest values on every load metric.
records.limitations: Only on-field tracking was analyzed, excluding sideline movement and collisions, and there are no injury or performance outcomes. Thresholds are relative to each position's own maximum velocity, so effort counts reflect relative rather than absolute intensity, and two authors are paid NFL consultants and four are NFL club employees.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read the position averages as training or return-to-play load targets, when they describe on-field game activity from one league's tracking system and say nothing about injury risk or individual readiness.

changes: evidenceSummary/tldr: 'wide receivers and defensive backs had the highest ... acceleration counts' -> WR highest, TE second (Table 2 acceleration efforts WR 65.7, TE 49.6, CB 42.3, LB 41.1, S 40.4)

paper.limitations: Discussion vs Table 2 conflict was described incompletely (LB 41.1 vs S 40.4) -> cornerbacks actually lead defense at 42.3 and safeties are lowest of the three ('On defense, S had the highest number of acceleration efforts, with LB closely following'); added the abstract vs Table 2 conflict on acceleration efforts; removed the unclear-n remark, since Table 2 reports player-games separately from the Methods' per-position player counts

populations: Professional / Elite confirmed by text ('professional American football athletes', 'these elite athletes'), not only inferred; added Male Athletes (Table 1 defines efforts relative to 'his positional maximum velocity')
verification.residualConcerns: Male Athletes rests on the pronoun 'his' in the metric definitions rather than an explicit sex statement. Funding and conflicts: two authors are paid NFL consultants and four are NFL club employees, and the work was supported by the NFL.

records.sourceFile: Preseason and in-season high speed running demands of 2 professional Australian Rules football teams.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Observational cohort analysis of GPS data from 55 male athletes at 2 professional Australian Rules football clubs, covering the 2019 preseason and the first 8 rounds of the season (4,174 training and match GPS files). Weekly running volume was greater in preseason than in-season in the 71 to 80% Vmax band (P < 0.01, r = 0.56) and the 81 to 90% Vmax band (P < 0.01, r = 0.58), but not in the 91 to 100% Vmax band (P = 0.10, r = 0.22). Individual variation was large, with coefficients of variation of 51%, 39% and 41% across the three bands.
records.limitations: Descriptive GPS data from two clubs in one season, with no injury, fitness or performance outcomes, so the study cannot show a protective or performance-enhancing running dose. Speed bands are relative to GPS-derived Vmax, and the abstract and Discussion describe the bands and significance differently from the Results.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could treat the preseason and in-season averages as a safe benchmark for sprint exposure, when the study has no injury or performance outcomes and only two clubs.

changes: limitations: added the Discussion inconsistency ('70% to 80%Vmax, 80% to 90%Vmax, and 90% to 100%Vmax all significantly (P < 0.05) lower in-season') vs Results P = 0.103, the abstract P = 0.01 vs Results P < 0.01, and the 'weekly' metric definition ('summed and then divided by the number of sessions in the respective week')
screeningLimitations: broadened band-label note to cover the Discussion inconsistency
verification.residualConcerns: Velocity band labels confirmed: abstract uses 'above 70%Vmax' and 'above 80%Vmax'; Results and Table 4 use 71-80%, 81-90% and 91-100% bands. Record reports the Results values.

records.sourceFile: Programing high-speed and sprint running exposure in football - Beliefs and practices of more than 100 practitioners worldwide.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Cross-sectional online survey of 102 football practitioners from 22 countries (data collected March to July 2022), covering beliefs and practices on high-speed and sprint running exposure, using descriptive statistics and mixed-effects and multinomial regression models. The authors report broad agreement on the importance of exposure, a lack of consensus on metric definitions and monitoring methods, and a probable link between match-outcome targets and the use of two microdosed sessions.
records.limitations: The sample is a convenience sample of practitioners (not athletes), mostly Italian and male, and reflects reported opinion rather than measured training or outcomes. The match-outcome model results were non-significant and the authors describe them as probable, so they should not be read as an established relationship.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read the authors' suggested scheduling of two sessions between MD+2 and MD-2 as an evidence-based standard, when it is a suggestion drawn from practitioner beliefs and a model with overlapping confidence intervals.
